{"id": "91:14/q02", "question": "Why does denial precede hamstringing, and how do the clauses connect?", "turns_on": "Whether fa marks event order, rhetorical sequence, or the answer to the earlier 'when' clause.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q02/p1", "position": "Denial preceded and prompted the hamstringing; fa gives sequence.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās insists fa places the slaughter after denial. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says denial caused the act. Al-Yamānī's natural ordering, quoted by al-Suyūṭī, puts rejection before slaughter. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads a second denial after the warning, while allowing a summary followed by detail."}, {"id": "91:14/q02/p2", "position": "The acts were concurrent or reversed in reality: hamstringing was itself denial.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and Ṭabarī allow ordering of closely linked cause and act either way; Ibn Qutayba expressly reads hamstringing first. Al-Naḥḥās argues against this because fa signals succession."}, {"id": "91:14/q02/p3", "position": "'They denied him' is complete; 'they hamstrung her' answers the earlier clause about the most wretched one rising.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ proposes this alternative; Ṭabarī and the grammarians he reports connect the second verb with 91:12. Al-Naḥḥās also accepts the completed first clause."}, {"id": "91:14/q02/p4", "position": "Fa can introduce details after a general statement, with intervening events.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī calls it explanatory. Ibn ʿĀshūr says textual sequence need not reproduce the event order, comparing 2:36 and 7:4."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q03", "question": "Had Thamūd ever believed Ṣāliḥ before this denial?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported early adherence occurred.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q03/p1", "position": "They remained unbelievers throughout.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān call this the majority view."}, {"id": "91:14/q03/p2", "position": "They followed Ṣāliḥ as Muslims for a time, then denied him and killed the camel.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this from a group; Abū Ḥayyān preserves it as an alternative to the majority."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q04", "question": "What does 'hamstrung her' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb's direct sense is the disabling cut or the resulting slaughter.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q04/p1", "position": "It means cutting a camel's legs or flesh so that blood flows and it falls for slaughter; killing follows by association.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī describe cutting into flesh and bloodshed; al-Ṭabrisī compares damage at an animal's root to a basin's base. Elmalılı specifies legs and tendons. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes wounding forelegs so the camel kneels for breast slaughter; Islahi says killing is the resultant, not primary, sense."}, {"id": "91:14/q04/p2", "position": "It means slaughtering or killing the she-camel.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives slaughter or killing as the sense; Study Quran reports commentators who render it slaughter, with 7:77–78. Asad refers to his note on 7:91 for his rendering without restating it here."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q05", "question": "Who hamstrung the camel, and why is the act attributed to all?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular culprit is the direct actor with collective consent or two men acted directly.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q05/p1", "position": "One direct killer acted with the people's approval or conspiracy, so all are charged.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says they agreed to deny water and consented to slaughter despite the alternating days. Qatāda reports pledges from young and old, men and women, before Qudār acted. Al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān compare 54:29 or 7:77. Qutb adds failure to stop him; Islahi says dissenting reformers were spared. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes the plural also follows Thamūd's collective grammar."}, {"id": "91:14/q05/p2", "position": "Two men performed the killing.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ reports two perpetrators; al-Qurṭubī explains that Arabic can use the singular superlative 'most wretched' for two."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q06", "question": "What names and descriptions are reported for the killer and accomplice?", "turns_on": "The reports preserve different names or descriptions and a literary comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q06/p1", "position": "The killer was Qudār or Qidār, a rebellious Thamūd leader.", "reasons": "Al-Suhaylī gives Qudār ibn Sālif and names his mother Qādira. Islahi calls Qidār autocratic; an Arabic couplet and al-Afwah's poetry make him a proverbial corrupt figure beside Qayl of ʿĀd."}, {"id": "91:14/q06/p2", "position": "Muṣda ibn Wihrāwa ibn Jahm was his accomplice.", "reasons": "Al-Suhaylī supplies the name in Bursevī's report."}, {"id": "91:14/q06/p3", "position": "A Prophetic report calls the camel's hamstringers the most wretched of earlier generations.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the Prophet's designation."}, {"id": "91:14/q06/p4", "position": "Aḥmar is named as culprit in a likely authentic poem, though elsewhere linked with ʿĀd.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says this may show overlapping tribal names or traditions; the poem has the calf's curse, not a divine warner or explicit command."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q07", "question": "What happened to the camel's calf after the slaughter?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q07/p1", "position": "It fled up a mountain and cried three times that its mother had been killed; the people could not seize it.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the people asked Ṣāliḥ what to do. Al-Ḥasan says it escaped to a mountain cleft and God struck their hearts."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q08", "question": "What warning, respite, and destruction followed the slaughter?", "turns_on": "The narrative reports specify different moments of the episode.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q08/p1", "position": "Ṣāliḥ gave three days marked by yellow, red, then black faces; punishment came on the fourth.", "reasons": "Muqātil links the three days to the calf's three cries. The people prepared graves, embalmed themselves, and first mistook the delay for mercy. Islahi also reports three days to repent, which increased arrogance."}, {"id": "91:14/q08/p2", "position": "Gabriel blocked the sun, cried, and their souls left as houses collapsed over their graves.", "reasons": "Muqātil places this on the fourth day and connects the ruined settlement to 11:68; Ibn al-Jawzī repeats the grave and collapsed-house account."}, {"id": "91:14/q08/p3", "position": "The camel was a demanded sign and a test with an assigned drinking turn.", "reasons": "Islahi cites 54:27–29 and says Ṣāliḥ gave it after their demand."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q09", "question": "How is fa-damdama read?", "turns_on": "The manuscripts and cited readers differ in consonants and wording; al-Jishumī restricts recitation to the established form.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q09/p1", "position": "The established widespread reading is fa-damdama.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says only this form may be recited despite Ibn al-Zubayr's variant; Abū Ḥayyān labels it the majority reading."}, {"id": "91:14/q09/p2", "position": "Ibn al-Zubayr reads fa-dahdama or a related hāʾ form.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says a codex has hāʾ between the dāls. Al-Qurṭubī calls the forms dialects, comparing imtaqa and intaqa; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī say its meaning matches the common reading. Abū Ḥayyān connects it with repeated covering."}, {"id": "91:14/q09/p3", "position": "Some codices read fa-dammara.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the codices and mentions it among manuscript variants."}, {"id": "91:14/q09/p4", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd's codex has fa-dammāhā ʿalayhim.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the reading and notes it again among variants."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q10", "question": "What does damdama mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is derived from covering, crushing, shaking, anger or sound, and how reduplication intensifies it.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q10/p1", "position": "It means punishment enclosing, covering, or overwhelming them.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj derives the sense from covering a grave or coating a fat camel; repetition strengthens it. Al-Rāzī compares coating every side and the doubled kabkabū. Al-Ālūsī analyzes the doubled form as faʿfal. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports grave-covering as the majority view but himself favors the sound of an angry cry."}, {"id": "91:14/q10/p2", "position": "It means destroying or annihilating them utterly.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ, Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Muʾarrij give destruction or complete extermination; al-Muʾarrij specifies that nothing is left. Al-Qāmūs gives total punishment or grinding a people. Ibn Khālawayh glosses it 'destroyed.'"}, {"id": "91:14/q10/p3", "position": "It means shaking or quaking the earth or a structure.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn al-Aʿrābī give the earthquake sense; al-Biqāʿī quotes al-Rāzī on shaking a building until it topples. Al-Wāḥidī calls this the view of most commentators."}, {"id": "91:14/q10/p4", "position": "It means leveling, crushing, or covering them with earth.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣiḥāḥ defines pressing an object to earth and crushing it; al-Qushayrī compares burial. Ibn ʿĀshūr says those who take this sense derive it from covering a grave. Corpus Coranicum prefers derivation from damma, 'level' or 'strike,' and says the anger/punishment glosses may be inferred from this verse."}, {"id": "91:14/q10/p5", "position": "It means divine anger, or the angry cry that destroyed them.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī also uses the word for speech that agitates someone. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the thunderclap and earthquake as God's angry shout; attributing it to God is figurative because He creates its sound, and he cites 15:73. Qutb says the sound of the word pictures terror."}, {"id": "91:14/q10/p6", "position": "It denotes repeated, intensified hardship or punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī compares the doubled forms dam and ṣarṣar. Al-Qurṭubī reads repeated enclosing as thorough destruction; al-Samīn also mentions an imitation of a collapse's sound and dye

{"id": "91:14/q11", "question": "What form or sound effect does damdama have?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish morphological repetition from sound symbolism.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q11/p1", "position": "It is a reduplicated quadriliteral that intensifies repeated covering or punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Rāzī compare doubled forms such as kabkabū. Al-Ālūsī calls the pattern faʿfal; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it faʿlala. Elmalılı derives it from damma, while al-Jishumī compares ṣarṣar."}, {"id": "91:14/q11/p2", "position": "Its sound evokes the violence and terror of the destruction.", "reasons": "Qutb says the word itself pictures divine wrath's terrifying scene; al-Samīn lists sound imitation of a collapse among its glosses."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q12", "question": "What does 'upon them' and 'their Lord' add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q12/p1", "position": "'Upon them' conveys punishment descending with encompassing severity.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī emphasizes its force and encirclement."}, {"id": "91:14/q12/p2", "position": "'Their Lord' recalls the benefactor they denied, heightening the withdrawal of favor and wrath.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī makes this contrast within the verse."}, {"id": "91:14/q12/p3", "position": "Naming the Lord resolves suspense created by the earlier indirect mā in the oath series.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the creator emerges enigmatically earlier and is named explicitly here."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q13", "question": "What does 'because of their sin' specify?", "turns_on": "The first explains the historical cause; the second explains why that cause is stated.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q13/p1", "position": "The bāʾ marks cause: the punishment came for their own denial, disbelief, and killing of the camel.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives the grammatical point. Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī list denial and slaughter; al-Biqāʿī stresses shared wrongdoing; Kuran Yolu says slaughter alone does not account for the judgment."}, {"id": "91:14/q13/p2", "position": "It explicitly warns every sinner that sin has consequences.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī calls Thamūd's fate a grave warning; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī say stating the cause even after fa universalizes the warning."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q14", "question": "To what does the pronoun in fa-sawwāhā refer, and what was leveled?", "turns_on": "The feminine suffix may resume the implied punishment, the tribe, or the earth; one report makes the leveling their houses onto graves.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q14/p1", "position": "It refers to the punishment or implied damdamah: God made it fall equally on everyone.", "reasons": "ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān and Ibn ʿĀshūr identify the implied feminine damdamah; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow punishment. Muqātil and al-Rāzī cite Gabriel's blast killing young and old. Elmalılı prefers this nearer feminine antecedent. Al-Biqāʿī adds strong and weak, killers and supporters, dying together; no one escaped."}, {"id": "91:14/q14/p2", "position": "It refers to Thamūd as a tribe: God leveled or annihilated them all.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī notes feminine agreement with the tribe name, as in ṭaghwāhā and ashqāhā; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says none survived. Al-Suddī and Yaḥyā ibn Sallām specify equal destruction of young and old. Ṭabrisī also reports people flattened uniformly into earth."}, {"id": "91:14/q14/p3", "position": "It refers to the earth or land: God flattened it over their bodies or dwellings.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites Ibn ʿAbbās on leveling the soil. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it hid bodies and dwellings, comparing 4:42. Elmalılı says the leveling reverses earlier fashioning; Qutb describes upper and lower land devastated."}, {"id": "91:14/q14/p4", "position": "God leveled their houses onto the graves they had dug and occupied.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the houses collapsed after Gabriel's cry; Ibn al-Jawzī preserves the same account, and Ibn Khālawayh calls their homes graves."}, {"id": "91:14/q14/p5", "position": "God made later nations equal to Thamūd.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this further possibility without an argument."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q15", "question": "How does the verse's wording connect destruction to creation earlier in the sūrah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q15/p1", "position": "Sawwā in verse 14 echoes the fashioning of the soul in verse 7.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it complete paronomasia. Corpus Coranicum reads the double use as sarcastic, linking moral obligation in creation to judgment; Study Quran says God destroys as readily as He creates and punishment continues the soul's fashioning. Elmalılı calls leveling a reversal of fashioning."}, {"id": "91:14/q15/p2", "position": "The leveling echoes the sun and the objects sworn by earlier.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī compares the leveled people with the sun in 91:1 and the subsequent oath objects."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q16", "question": "What does the Thamūd episode do in the sūrah's argument and oath?", "turns_on": "The notes identify either an implied oath answer and threat or the story's broader moral and historical function.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q16/p1", "position": "It warns Quraysh that rejecting Muhammad risks destruction like Thamūd's rejection of Ṣāliḥ.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī makes this the oath's answer and treats 'he succeeds' as an aside. Ibn ʿĀshūr also makes Thamūd's destruction the implied answer, its lām omitted after a long oath as in al-Burūj; he says the warning addressed arrogant Quraysh and recalls their sword punishment. Islahi says Quraysh leaders' reported plot against Muhammad sharpens the warning."}, {"id": "91:14/q16/p2", "position": "It exemplifies humanity's choice between good and evil and the destruction of a rebellious community.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum calls it the oldest genuine Quranic punishment legend and suggests it may mirror the preacher's rejection. Kuran Yolu links it to the moral choice and to al-Aʿrāf and Hūd. Islahi says historical examples move ordinary hearers alongside cosmic and inward proofs."}, {"id": "91:14/q16/p3", "position": "Thamūd alone suffices because its history was familiar to Quraysh.", "reasons": "Islahi quotes Farāhī that the allusion evoked inherited settlements and traditions; he cites Arab poetry about Qidār and says the rebellion and fate were proverbial."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q17", "question": "What does the verse teach about collective responsibility and divine judgment?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish social accountability, justice, and the camel's role as a sign.", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q17/p1", "position": "A community shares worldly punishment when it collectively approves or fails to restrain wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Qutb calls this a principle of social accountability and says neglect of mutual counsel is culpable; he preserves individual judgment in the afterlife. Islahi likewise separates collective worldly punishment from individual final judgment and says reformers or dissenters are spared. Al-Biqāʿī includes consenting supporters in the simultaneous punishment."}, {"id": "91:14/q17/p2", "position": "God's destruction of the guilty is just.", "reasons": "Elmalılı argues that creation, restoration, and recompense belong to God, so annihilation does not harm Him or wrong them. Islahi says a nation receives time and clear warning before collective destruction."}, {"id": "91:14/q17/p3", "position": "The punishment answers deliberate harm to a divine sign after warning.", "reasons": "Islahi says the camel tested the nation; further delay risked murder of the Messenger, a crime bringing national destruction. Kuran Yolu stresses persistent rejection beyond the slaughter."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q18", "question": "How is this Thamūd account related to other accounts and traditions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q18/p1", "position": "The Qur'anic allusion reworks an earlier camel story around a divine messenger, command, and ethical rejection.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares Umayya's likely authentic poem, which has cultic disrespect and a calf's curse but no divine warner; the Quran omits a lame survivor's aftermath because it does not serve the general lesson. It places Q 91 alongside 89, 85, and 105 as early narrative texts, with fuller Thamūd material later in Q 54 and shorter references in 69 and 51."}, {"id": "91:14/q18/p2", "position": "Other Quranic passages describe the catastrophe as a cry, earthquake, or humiliating thunderbolt.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites 15:73, 15:83, 23:41, 7:78, 7:91, 29:37, and 41:17; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the cry in 15:73."}, {"id": "91:14/q18/p3", "position": "The repeated kadhdhaba foregrounds rejection of the messenger as the immediate cause.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum connects verse 14 with verse 11 and Syriac kaddeb, directing readers also to 95:7, 92:16, and 73:11."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q19", "question": "How may verse 14 be divided in verse counting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q19/p1", "position": "A verse break after ʿaqarūhā fits the offense and punishment divide and the rhyme.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum attributes this to the Ḥimṣ, Mecca b and Medina I traditions, noting that Ḥimṣ lacks a break after sawwāhā where the rhyme calls for one."}]}

{"id": "91:14/q22", "question": "How does the camel warning supply the context for this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q22/p1", "position": "The earlier command implies preserving the camel and its drinking right, with threatened punishment for harming her.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies omitted imperatives such as 'preserve,' 'leave,' or 'beware' and points to other sūra accounts of the camel."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q23", "question": "How does the following clause connect after fa-sawwāhā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q23/p1", "position": "Wāw begins a new sentence; fāʾ instead links the clauses in sequence.", "reasons": "Ibn Khālawayh says the fear in 'he does not fear its consequence' is not the people's act, so wāw starts anew, while fāʾ presents a continued order."}]}
{"id": "91:14/q24", "question": "How is Thamūd's transgression in the preceding verse read and understood?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "91:14/q24/p1", "position": "Ṭughyān means exceeding the bounds in corruption; some read bi-ṭughwā with ḍamma as a feminine verbal noun.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives the lexical sense and reports al-Ḥasan and Ḥammād ibn Maslama's ḍamma reading, comparing feminine verbal nouns rajʿā and ḥusnā."}]}
{"id": "92:4/q01", "question": "What does سَعْيَكُمْ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word names human action itself or the consequences it brings.", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q01/p1", "position": "People's work, deeds, or purposeful pursuits.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzi give its basic sense as quick walking, below running; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls its use for work metaphorical. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ adds persistence and directed purpose, citing 20:20, 20:66, 66:8, 57:12 for literal or figurative movement, 21:94, 17:19, 18:104 for sustained work, and 2:114, 5:33, 5:64, 76:22, 53:40, 88:9 for directed aims. Jishumī includes earning; Corpus Coranicum compares 88:8, 76:22, 53:39. Ṭabāṭabāʾī combines swift walking with purposeful deeds. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ikrima, and Muḥammad b. Kaʿb simply gloss it as action or deeds."}, {"id": "92:4/q01/p2", "position": "The consequences of people's effort.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī cites 53:39–40 and explicitly takes saʿy as the consequence of effort rather than effort itself."}]}
{"id": "92:4/q02", "question": "Who is addressed by كُمْ?", "turns_on": "Whether the address is treated as general or situated among Meccans.", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q02/p1", "position": "All people, including believers and unbelievers, especially people accountable for their acts.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly includes both groups; Biqāʿī identifies morally accountable people. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says direct general address supports a universal lesson, and Rāzī cites 92:4 and 92:14 for general scope."}, {"id": "92:4/q02/p2", "position": "The people of Mecca.", "reasons": "Muqātil locates the contrast in Meccan deeds, good and evil; al-Wāḥidī transmits this formulation."}]}
{"id": "92:4/q03", "question": "Why call human activity سَعْي?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q03/p1", "position": "The word evokes exertion and persistent work directed toward an aim.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says each person puts utmost effort into work. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ explains its literal walking sense and the sustained, purposeful work it implies, illustrating directed aims with 2:114, 5:33, 5:64, 76:22, 53:40, 88:9."}]}
{"id": "92:4/q04", "question": "What does شَتَّىٰ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether separation here means variation between pursuits or the disarray of efforts.", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q04/p1", "position": "Different, separate, or far apart.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Qatāda, and many others gloss it as diverse. Jishumī links its family of words to distance and division; Ṭabrisī compares shattān for distant things; Qurṭubī says unlike deeds are far apart. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes shattā, variation opposed to concord, from ashtāt, scattering opposed to gathering, citing 99:6, 59:14, 24:61 and the Qurʾanic uses for plants, efforts, and divided hearts. Wāḥidī points to varied plants at 20:53; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites a line by Taʾabbaṭa Sharran on diverse destinations and paths."}, {"id": "92:4/q04/p2", "position": "Scattered, disordered, or fragmented.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reads this as uncoordinated human effort; he connects dispersion to the call to hold together in 3:103. Other glosses also use 'scattered' without his social inference."}]}
{"id": "92:4/q05", "question": "What is the form and predication of شَتَّىٰ?", "turns_on": "How a plural or abstract description is predicated of the singular verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q05/p1", "position": "It is the plural of شَتِيت, predicated of a collectively plural سَعْي.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Iṣlāḥī give the singular shatīt; Qurṭubī compares marīḍ/marḍā and Biqāʿī qatīl/qatlā. Ālūsī says the annexed generic verbal noun includes all endeavors, explaining its plural predicate."}, {"id": "92:4/q05/p2", "position": "It may function as an abstract or feminine verbal noun meaning separation.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports the abstract-noun analysis and says treating the striving as separation itself heightens the assertion."}, {"id": "92:4/q05/p3", "position": "It may imply a possessive term: effort possessing separation.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports a predicate with an implied dhū or dhāt."}, {"id": "92:4/q05/p4", "position": "It may be an adjective meaning scattered.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports the adjectival analysis."}]}

{"id": "92:4/q09", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from differing striving?", "turns_on": "Whether the inner difference is a hierarchy of aims, a prior allotment of stations, or the lack of inward acceptance despite outward goods.", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q09/p1", "position": "Striving spans ranks of sincerity, intention, nearness, and orientation toward God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ ranges from speech or deed to intention, heart and action, worldly aims, afterlife aims, and God alone; 43:32 illustrates allotted ranks and the highest Godward striving is not lost. {"id": "92:4/q10", "question": "What does differing striving imply about God's decree and human acts?", "turns_on": "How divine decree and moral responsibility are related in the opposing human acts.", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q10/p1", "position": "Divergent good and evil acts occur under God's inspiration, creation, and prior decree.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zubayr ties divergence to God's eternal decree and testing and to purified and corrupted souls at 91:10; he cites inspiration at 91:8, human deeds created by God at 37:96, and God's being unquestioned at 21:23, opposing Qadariyya and Muʿtazila. {"id": "92:4/q11", "question": "What event is reported behind the contrast of efforts?", "turns_on": "Which named people and transaction the reported occasion identifies; one Bilāl account also varies the payment amount.", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q11/p1", "position": "Abū Bakr's freeing of Bilāl is contrasted with Umayya and Ubayy, sons of Khalaf, who tortured him.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's reports say Abū Bakr bought Bilāl and freed him for God; Māwardī specifies a cloak and ten coins, while Elmalılı says a cloak and ten uqiyyas. {"id": "92:4/q12", "question": "Does the verse's lesson extend beyond its reported occasion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q12/p1", "position": "Yes; the address and warning apply generally to human efforts.", "reasons": "Al-Qaffāl says the Abū Bakr and Umayya context has a general message; Rāzī points to 92:4 and the warning at 92:14. {"id": "92:4/q13", "question": "How do the opening oaths relate to this statement?", "turns_on": "Whether the oath pairs chiefly frame moral contrast or demonstrate the paired structure of this life and the Hereafter.", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q13/p1", "position": "Visible opposed pairs foreshadow opposed human deeds and their outcomes.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says the oaths' opposites match human good and evil. Al-Sāmarrāʾī adds opposed times, agents, states, and destinations."}, {"id": "92:4/q13/p2", "position": "The creation's paired order points to an afterlife counterpart and a necessary Judgment.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the outer and inner worlds establish an afterlife; otherwise creation lacks purpose and the righteous and wrongdoers would be equal, contrary to divine wisdom."}]}
{"id": "92:4/q14", "question": "Why do the oaths say male and female rather than 'the pair'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q14/p1", "position": "The separate terms stress difference, while 'the pair' suggests likeness and union.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts al-Layl with al-Qiyāma and al-Najm, which discuss embryonic development and divine power; he cites 75:37–39, 53:43–45, 38:58, and 30:21."}]}
{"id": "92:4/q15", "question": "What wording of the preceding oath is reported from Ibn Masʿūd?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q15/p1", "position": "His reading says 'the day when it shines' and 'the male and the female,' omitting 'what He created.'", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits this through Abū Isḥāq from ʿAbd Allāh; the variant concerns the oath to which 92:4 responds."}]}
{"id": "92:4/q16", "question": "How does this statement lead into the following verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:4/q16/p1", "position": "It summarizes divergent efforts before the following verses specify the contrasting paths and fates.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ say the later verses explain shattā. {"id": "92:5/q01", "question": "What does fa-ammā do in the argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q01/p1", "position": "It introduces a conditional division of the preceding statement that human efforts differ.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says tafṣīl separates a shared group by a relevant difference; the account moves eloquently from efforts to their agents. {"id": "92:5/q02", "question": "Who is the giver described here?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports identify a particular occasion or the unrestricted relative pronoun is taken generally.", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q02/p1", "position": "The description applies to everyone who has these traits, including the named examples.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses the general force of man; al-Ālūsī says general wording governs despite particular occasions. Rāzī cites the general statements about varied striving and the Fire at 92:4,14. Jishumī says the passage's point is general. Kur'an Yolu applies both message and rulings generally."}, {"id": "92:5/q02/p2", "position": "The giver is Abū Bakr.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd and most commentators identify him; reports describe freeing weak enslaved Muslims or Bilāl, seeking God's reward rather than strong protectors. {"id": "92:5/q03", "question": "What does giving mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the gift is wealth in general, required financial dues, wider obedience and rights, or an inward gift.", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q03/p1", "position": "Giving wealth in good causes, both required and voluntary.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī specifies God's commanded ways and what God bestowed; Ibn ʿAbbās sometimes says one's available or surplus wealth. Rāzī names manumission, captive ransom and support for Muslims, with 2:3, 8:3, 76:8 and 92:17–20; Elm alılı adds feeding the needy. Al-Ālūsī understands these as financial obligations. Al-Ālūsī rejects the obedience reading as contrary to conventional money-giving and the contrast with withholding."}, {"id": "92:5/q03/p4", "position": "Giving means offering truth to God from the heart.", "reasons": "This reading is attributed to al-Ḥasan by Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī."}, {"id": "92:5/q03/p5", "position": "Giving is an inward relinquishment for God's pleasure.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī says the generous give up both abodes, avoid frivolity and doubtful matters and persist toward nearness; al-Qāshānī adds purifying attachment to what was relinquished."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q04", "question": "Why are the objects of 'gave' omitted?", "turns_on": "Whether the omission highlights the giver or leaves the kind and recipient of giving open.", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q04/p1", "position": "The omission makes the deed and giver the focus of praise.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says both gift and recipient are omitted because praise concerns the giver; al-Samīn includes omissions after 'was mindful' and 'affirmed,' and parallel omissions in the opposing clause. {"id": "92:5/q05", "question": "What does being mindful mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether its scope is God and disobedience generally, stinginess specifically, the Day or reckoning, or inward detachment.", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q05/p1", "position": "Fearing God and guarding against disobedience or His punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī connects protection with obedience and avoiding sin. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ gives the root sense of protection from harm, adduces 16:81 and verses locating piety in the heart (22:32,37; 49:3; 58:9), and its contrast with wickedness (91:8; 38:28). {"id": "92:5/q06", "question": "What is understood as the object of 'was mindful'?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted object is God, the Day or reckoning, or left open.", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q06/p1", "position": "God is the understood object.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr supplies God; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says that when the Qurʾān states the object of taqwā it is God."}, {"id": "92:5/q06/p2", "position": "The Day of Judgment is understood.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares the explicit construction in 73:17 and prefers it for the absolute verb here."}, {"id": "92:5/q06/p3", "position": "The omitted object keeps protection general, with stinginess especially in view.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguishes an unspecified use from an ellipsis that requires recovering a particular object."}]}

{"id": "92:5/q08", "question": "How do these descriptions explain the sura's contrast?", "turns_on": "Whether the division emphasizes agents and traits, outcomes, or the structure joining both.", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q08/p1", "position": "They unpack the preceding claim that human striving differs into opposed paths and outcomes.", "reasons": "Rāzī pairs deeds with reward or punishment; al-Bayḍāwī says the descriptions explain divergent efforts.
